analogy.p: Imagine a buoy bobbing on sea waves, connected to a coil that slides in and out of a magnet. The sea wave is the sound wave, the buoy is the diaphragm, and the generator coil is the microphone's coil: the waves push the buoy up and down, the coil moves through the magnetic field, and electricity is produced in step with the waves. Bigger waves give more electricity; faster waves give a faster alternating current. It breaks down because sound is a pressure (longitudinal) wave, not a height wave, because a microphone's movements are tiny (fractions of a millimetre), and because the microphone's output is a faint signal rather than usable power.
analogy.t: A wave-energy buoy driving a generator

bullets: It sits between waves (4.6 – sound as a longitudinal wave) and electromagnetism (4.7 – the generator and motor effects).
Key idea in one line: **sound → vibrating diaphragm → moving coil in a magnetic field → induced alternating pd → signal to an amplifier**.
A microphone is an **input transducer**: it converts one form of energy (the kinetic energy of vibrating air and diaphragm) into an electrical signal.
The generator effect is **induction**: a pd is induced whenever a conductor and a magnetic field move relative to each other so that magnetic field lines are cut.
You must always name the **generator effect** (not the motor effect) when explaining a microphone. Examiners reward the correct term.
Since it is Physics only, Combined Science students do not need this, but Physics GCSE students can be asked it on either Paper 2 (magnetism is a Paper 2 topic).
core.h: What the specification asks and where it fits
core.p: This is a **Physics-only** (triple science) idea from AQA 4.7 Magnetism and electromagnetism, in the part about uses of the **generator effect**. The specification wants you to be able to explain how, in a **moving-coil microphone**, the pressure variations of a sound wave make a diaphragm move, how that moves a coil of wire in a magnetic field, and how this produces an **alternating potential difference** (and so an alternating current if the circuit is complete). Alongside it, you need to be able to contrast it with a **loudspeaker**, which uses the **motor effect** in reverse. The topic is a favourite for 4 to 6 mark 'explain how' questions because the logical chain has several linked steps, and each step is a mark.

bullets: Definition to learn: **the generator effect is when a potential difference is induced across a conductor which is moving relative to a magnetic field (or in a changing magnetic field).**
If the circuit is complete, a current is induced; if it is not, there is still a pd across the ends of the wire but no current.
**No movement, no pd**: if the coil stops, the induced pd falls to zero even if the magnet is strong.
**Reverse the direction of movement** and the direction of the induced pd (and current) reverses.
Reversing the magnet's poles (swapping N and S) also reverses the direction of the induced pd.
Moving the magnet into a coil is equivalent to moving the coil over the magnet: only the **relative motion** matters.

Extension idea: the induced current creates its own magnetic field which **opposes** the change that produced it. That is why it takes effort to push a magnet into a coil that is part of a complete circuit (energy is conserved).
core.h: Recap: the generator effect (the physics behind the microphone)
core.p: The **generator effect** is the name for the production of a **potential difference across a conductor** when there is **relative movement between the conductor and a magnetic field**, or when the **magnetic field through a conductor changes**. If the conductor is part of a complete circuit, the induced pd drives an **induced current**. The effect works because the conductor 'cuts' magnetic field lines: the free electrons inside the metal experience a force as the wire moves through the field, so charge is pushed along the wire, creating a pd. The cause must be a change: a coil sitting still in a steady field gives no pd at all.

bullets: Compression: particles squashed together, pressure higher than normal. Rarefaction: particles spread apart, pressure lower than normal.
**Higher frequency → higher pitch**; **larger amplitude → louder sound**.
Wave speed equation: **wave speed (m/s) = frequency (Hz) × wavelength (m)**, v = f λ. Speed of sound in air is about 340 m/s.
Period: **T = 1 / f**, with T in seconds and f in hertz. A 250 Hz note has period 1/250 = 0.004 s.
A microphone must respond fast enough to follow the vibrations, so its moving parts must have **very low mass** (a thin, light diaphragm and a small coil).
The electrical signal produced is an **analogue copy** of the sound: it rises and falls in step with the pressure changes.
core.h: Recap: sound waves and what a microphone has to detect
core.p: Sound is a **longitudinal wave**: the particles of the air vibrate **parallel** to the direction the wave travels, producing alternating regions of high pressure (**compressions**) and low pressure (**rarefactions**). A sound wave transfers energy through the air but the air itself does not travel from the source to your ear. A microphone has to detect those rapid pressure changes. The **frequency** of the wave (number of waves per second, in hertz, Hz) decides the **pitch**, and the **amplitude** (the maximum pressure variation, which sets how large the vibration is) decides the **loudness**. Humans hear roughly 20 Hz to 20 000 Hz.

bullets: **Diaphragm**: thin, light, flexible membrane. It must be light so it can respond quickly to high-frequency sounds.
**Coil of wire**: many turns of thin insulated copper wire, glued to the diaphragm. More turns means a larger induced pd.
**Permanent magnet**: usually shaped so the coil sits in a narrow gap where the field is strong and perpendicular to the wire. Its field is steady (the field is not changing).
**Leads**: the ends of the coil are connected to an external circuit. Without a complete circuit there is a pd but no current.
The magnet is fixed and the coil moves, which is the reverse arrangement to some dynamos but the physics is identical because relative motion is what matters.
The microphone has **no battery** supplying the signal: the energy for the electrical signal comes from the sound wave itself (which is why the output is tiny).
core.p: A moving-coil microphone has four essential parts working together: a **diaphragm**, a **coil of wire** fixed to the diaphragm, a **permanent magnet**, and wires leading to an external circuit (usually an **amplifier**). The diaphragm is a thin, light, flexible sheet that is pushed and pulled by the pressure variations of a sound wave. The coil is attached to the back of the diaphragm so that it moves with it. The coil sits in the gap of a permanent magnet, which provides a **strong, steady magnetic field**. The magnet does not move; only the diaphragm and coil move.

bullets: Step 1: **sound waves (pressure variations) hit the diaphragm** and make it vibrate with the same frequency as the sound.
Step 2: the **coil, attached to the diaphragm, moves back and forth** in the magnetic field of the permanent magnet.
Step 3: the coil **cuts magnetic field lines**, so a **potential difference is induced** (generator effect).
Step 4: because the coil moves **in then out**, the direction of the induced pd keeps **reversing**: it is an **alternating pd**, which drives an **alternating current** in the circuit.
Step 5: the **frequency of the alternating current equals the frequency of the sound wave**.
Step 6: the signal is very small, so it is fed to an **amplifier** and then to a recording device, transmitter or loudspeaker.
Energy transfer: **kinetic energy of the vibrating air/diaphragm → electrical energy**.
core.h: How it works: the full step-by-step explanation
core.p: Examiners mark this as a chain of cause and effect, so learn the order. Sound waves arrive at the diaphragm and the pressure on the diaphragm alternates. During a compression the pressure is higher than the pressure on the other side, so the diaphragm is pushed inwards; during a rarefaction the pressure is lower and the diaphragm moves outwards (springs back). Because the coil is attached to the diaphragm, the coil moves backwards and forwards **through the magnetic field of the permanent magnet**. The coil therefore cuts magnetic field lines, and by the generator effect a pd is induced across the ends of the coil.

bullets: Moving in → pd one direction; moving out → pd in the opposite direction. This is exactly the rule that reversing the motion reverses the pd.
The graph of pd against time has the same **shape and frequency** as the diaphragm's displacement pattern (the sound wave), so it is a faithful 'copy'.
The pd is zero when the coil momentarily stops at the extremes of its motion and has maximum size when it passes the central position at greatest speed.
A **single steady tone** (one frequency) gives a **sine-shaped** trace; real speech or music gives a complicated trace made of many frequencies added together.
The signal is not mains-like: its frequency can be anything from tens of hertz to thousands of hertz, not just 50 Hz.
This is why the output is described as an **alternating current (a.c.)** – never 'direct current'.
core.h: Why the output is an alternating current
core.p: The direction of the induced pd depends on the direction in which the coil moves through the field. When the coil moves inwards the induced pd drives current one way round the circuit. When it moves outwards the induced pd is reversed, so the current flows the other way round. Because the diaphragm vibrates continually in and out, the pd keeps switching direction, producing an **alternating pd** that changes in step with the vibration. When the coil is momentarily at rest at the end of each swing, the induced pd is zero, and it is largest when the coil is moving fastest, through the middle of its motion.

bullets: **Higher frequency (pitch)** → diaphragm vibrates faster → **more cycles per second** on the pd trace (waves squashed closer together).
**Greater amplitude (loudness)** → larger vibration → coil moves faster → **greater maximum pd** (taller waves).
A very quiet sound gives a very small pd, which is why amplification is essential.
Pitch and loudness are independent: you can have a loud low note or a quiet high note.
The trace on an oscilloscope: **vertical axis = pd (V)**, **horizontal axis = time (s)**. Use the horizontal axis to find the period and frequency; use the vertical axis to compare amplitudes.
If a sound is twice as loud in amplitude the trace is roughly twice as tall; if the frequency doubles the period halves so twice as many waves fit across the screen.
core.h: Loudness and pitch in the electrical signal
core.p: Two properties of the sound must be reproduced faithfully, and each corresponds to one feature of the pd-time graph. The **pitch** (frequency) of the sound decides how quickly the diaphragm vibrates, so it sets how many complete cycles of pd occur each second: a higher pitch gives **more waves per second** on the trace. The **loudness** (amplitude) of the sound decides how far, and how fast, the diaphragm and coil move: a louder sound makes bigger movements at higher speed, so the coil cuts field lines faster and a **larger pd** is induced. That is why a loud sound gives a **taller trace** (greater amplitude).

bullets: **Faster movement** → field lines cut at a greater rate → larger pd. For a microphone this means a louder sound or a higher frequency vibration of the same size.
**Stronger magnet** → more field lines per unit area to cut → larger pd.
**More turns on the coil** → each turn contributes → larger total pd (pd roughly proportional to the number of turns).
A larger coil area in the field cuts more field lines.
Making the coil heavier would reduce how fast it can move in response to sound, so there is a design compromise: lots of turns but low mass.
Be careful in exam wording: say 'cuts the field lines **faster**' or 'greater rate of change of magnetic field', not just 'moves more'.
core.h: What affects the size of the induced pd
core.p: The size of the induced pd depends on how quickly the magnetic field through the coil is changing, which means how fast the coil cuts field lines. Three things can be changed to produce a larger pd: **move the coil faster** (relative to the field), use a **stronger magnetic field**, or use a **coil with more turns**. Each turn of wire gets its own induced pd and the turns are in series, so the pds add together. A larger area of coil in the field also helps because more field lines are cut. These are exactly the same factors as for any generator, which is why generator questions and microphone questions test the same ideas.

bullets: Microphone: **sound → electrical**; **generator effect**; movement causes the pd.
Loudspeaker: **electrical → sound**; **motor effect**; current causes the movement.
Both have a **coil, a permanent magnet and a thin cone/diaphragm**.
In a loudspeaker the current has a frequency equal to the sound frequency; in a microphone the induced current frequency equals the sound frequency – the same relationship, reversed.
A small loudspeaker can actually be used as a poor microphone (and vice versa) because both rely on the same arrangement.
Headphones work like tiny loudspeakers (motor effect, coil, magnet, diaphragm).
core.h: Microphone versus loudspeaker: opposite energy transfers
core.p: A **loudspeaker** is almost the same device as a moving-coil microphone, but run in reverse. In a loudspeaker an **alternating current** from an amplifier flows through a coil placed in a permanent magnetic field. The **motor effect** produces a force on the coil (F = BIl), and because the current alternates the force alternates in direction, so the coil and the paper cone attached to it move backwards and forwards. This vibrates the air and produces a **sound wave** of the same frequency as the current. So a microphone turns sound into an electrical signal using the generator effect, and a loudspeaker turns an electrical signal into sound using the motor effect.

bullets: Amplifier: increases the **amplitude** of the signal while keeping the **frequency** the same. (Pitch stays the same; loudness increases.)
Typical use chain: **sound → microphone → amplifier → loudspeaker → louder sound**.
The signal can be converted to digital form for recording or broadcast.
Because the signal is tiny, interference (noise) can be picked up, so microphone leads are often shielded.
Microphones are used in phones, public address systems, recording studios, hearing aids and intercoms.
The final loudspeaker converts the amplified electrical signal back into sound energy.
core.h: Why an amplifier is needed and what happens to the signal next
core.p: The induced pd from a microphone is small, typically only a few millivolts, because the diaphragm moves tiny distances (fractions of a millimetre) and the only energy source is the sound wave itself. The weak a.c. signal is sent to an **amplifier**, which increases its amplitude (the size of the pd) without changing its frequency, so the sound is reproduced louder but at the same pitch. The amplified signal can then be recorded, transmitted by cable or radio waves, or sent to a loudspeaker to be turned back into sound. Without amplification a loudspeaker could not be driven.

bullets: **Frequency = 1 ÷ period**; **period = 1 ÷ frequency**. Check that time is in seconds before doing the division (convert ms: 4 ms = 0.004 s).
Example: 5 complete waves in 20 ms → T = 20 ÷ 5 = 4 ms = 0.004 s → f = 1 ÷ 0.004 = **250 Hz**.
Example: λ of a 250 Hz sound with speed 340 m/s: λ = 340 ÷ 250 = **1.36 m**.
Amplitude is measured from the **centre line to the peak**, not peak to trough.
If the trace is twice as tall at the same frequency, the sound has the same pitch but is louder.
If twice as many waves fit in the same time, frequency is doubled: higher pitch.
core.h: Reading pd-time traces and doing calculations
core.p: Exam questions often show an oscilloscope trace or a pd-time graph from a microphone and ask you to find the **period**, the **frequency** or to compare two traces. To find the frequency, first measure the **time for one complete wave** (the period, T) using the horizontal scale and then use **f = 1 / T**. If you see several waves, divide the total time by the number of waves to get T. To compare loudness, compare the heights (amplitudes). Always include units: seconds for T, hertz for f, volts or millivolts for pd. For wave speed problems, use **v = f λ**, rearranged as f = v / λ or λ = v / f.

bullets: **Dynamo/alternator**: same induction principle, but the coil or magnet rotates continuously; a microphone's coil just vibrates.
**Transformer**: also uses electromagnetic induction, but with a changing field from an alternating current rather than moving parts.
**Motor effect**: F = BIl is used in loudspeakers; the generator effect is the microphone's partner.
**Energy**: only the energy in the sound wave is available, so the electrical output power is small.
**Conservation of energy**: the induced current opposes the motion (Lenz); that opposing force is why energy has to be put in to get electrical energy out.
**Waves**: sound can be recorded as an electrical signal and later reproduced because the signal copies the wave's frequency and amplitude.
core.h: Links to other topics and Higher tier extension
core.p: The microphone is a neat bridge between several parts of the course. It uses **sound as a longitudinal wave**, **electromagnetic induction** (generator effect), and the idea that **energy is transferred, not created**. The same physics gives dynamos and alternators, where a coil rotates in a field, and transformers, where a changing field in one coil induces a pd in another. At Higher level you can also explain why the induced current in a closed circuit opposes the motion that created it: the induced current produces its own magnetic field which pushes back against the coil's motion, so work done moving the coil becomes electrical energy. It also links to the motor effect, because the loudspeaker is the reverse device.

bullets: Too heavy a diaphragm/coil → cannot follow high-frequency sounds → poor high-pitch response.
Too stiff a diaphragm → small movement → very weak signal.
Strong permanent magnets (often neodymium in modern devices) increase the field strength and the output.
Used in: phones, karaoke, studio recording, hearing aids, security intercoms and speech recognition devices.
Because pd is only induced while the coil is moving, a microphone gives no output in silence (apart from background noise).
Moving-coil types are robust and don't need a battery, which makes them popular for live performances.
core.p: A real microphone is a compromise. The diaphragm needs to be **light and flexible** to respond to high frequencies, but strong enough not to tear. The coil needs **many turns** for a large signal but not so heavy that it cannot follow rapid vibrations. The magnet has to give a strong field in the gap. Because the only energy comes from the sound wave, the signal is small. Microphones are therefore designed to pick up the range of frequencies most important for speech and music, roughly 20 Hz to 20 kHz, matching human hearing.

exam: **Command words**: 'Explain how' needs a chain of reasons (cause → effect → effect); 'Describe' only needs what happens; 'Compare' needs similarities and differences about both devices.

**4-mark microphone explanation** – a model mark scheme: sound waves make the diaphragm vibrate (1); the coil attached to it moves in the magnetic field of the magnet (1); a potential difference is induced across the coil / generator effect (1); the direction of movement keeps changing so an alternating current is produced with the same frequency as the sound (1).
Always name the **generator effect** and state that the coil **cuts the magnetic field lines**. Examiners often make this the key mark.
For 'why does it produce a.c.?' write: **'the coil moves in and out so the direction of the induced pd keeps reversing'**.
For 'how could the output be made bigger?' give three: **stronger magnet, more turns on the coil, a louder sound or faster movement**. Link each to 'more field lines cut per second'.

For **6-mark questions** (e.g. compare microphone and loudspeaker): cover structure (coil, magnet, diaphragm/cone), the effect used (generator vs motor), the energy transfer (sound→electrical vs electrical→sound), the direction of cause and effect, and frequency relationship. Aim for a logical order: 'In a microphone... In a loudspeaker...'.
**Graph tips**: label axes (pd/V against time/s). Amplitude from centre line to peak. Compare traces by height (loudness) and number of waves (pitch).
**Calculation tips**: show f = 1/T or v = fλ, convert time to seconds, give units (Hz, m). Write the equation first for marks even if the arithmetic goes wrong.
Avoid vague words like 'it makes electricity' or 'the sound goes in the coil'. Say 'a potential difference is induced'.

A common 1-mark question: 'Name the effect that allows a microphone to work' → **generator effect** (Physics only). Another: 'Why is an amplifier needed?' → the signal from the microphone is very small.

mistakes.r: A microphone works by the generator effect (induction): movement of a coil in a magnetic field induces a pd. The motor effect is used in the loudspeaker.
mistakes.w: A microphone works by the motor effect.

mistakes.r: The magnet is fixed. The sound moves the diaphragm and the coil attached to it, which moves relative to the magnet.
mistakes.w: The sound makes the magnet move.

mistakes.r: The coil moves in and out so the direction of the induced pd reverses: it is an alternating current.
mistakes.w: The coil makes a direct current.

mistakes.r: A louder sound gives a larger amplitude; pitch (frequency) is unchanged. Higher frequency means higher pitch.
mistakes.w: A louder sound gives a higher frequency signal.

mistakes.r: The sound wave makes the diaphragm vibrate; the movement of the coil in the field induces the pd. Say the energy is transferred by the generator effect.
mistakes.w: The sound wave itself becomes the electricity.

mistakes.r: No battery is needed. The signal is induced by the relative motion; the energy comes from the sound wave.
mistakes.w: The microphone has a battery that creates the signal.

mistakes.r: The pd is only induced while there is relative movement; when the coil is stationary there is no induced pd.
mistakes.w: A stronger signal means the coil has stopped.

mistakes.r: An amplifier increases the amplitude (pd) but keeps the same frequency, so the pitch stays the same.
Frequency = 1 ÷ period; and always convert ms to seconds first.

summary: You need to be able to explain how a moving-coil microphone uses the generator effect to turn sound waves into an alternating electrical signal: pressure variations make a diaphragm and attached coil move in a magnetic field, which induces an alternating potential difference with the same frequency as the sound. It is a Physics-only topic that joins together waves (sound), magnetism and electromagnetic induction, and it is the exact reverse of how a loudspeaker works.

terms.d: The induction of a potential difference across a conductor which is moving relative to a magnetic field, or in a changing magnetic field.
The energy transferred per unit charge between two points, measured in volts (V); the 'push' that drives current.
Current that repeatedly reverses direction; its direction changes continually with time.
A device with a diaphragm joined to a coil that moves in the field of a permanent magnet, transferring sound energy into an electrical signal.
A thin, light, flexible sheet that vibrates when sound waves hit it.
A wave in which the oscillations of the particles are parallel to the direction of energy transfer; sound in air is longitudinal.
A region of a longitudinal wave where particles are squashed together and the pressure is higher than normal.
A region of a longitudinal wave where particles are spread apart and the pressure is lower than normal.
The number of complete waves passing a point (or the number of cycles per second); measured in hertz (Hz).
The time taken for one complete wave or cycle; T = 1 / f, measured in seconds.
The maximum displacement of a wave from its undisturbed (rest) position; for sound it determines loudness, for a pd trace the maximum pd.
How high or low a sound seems, which is determined by its frequency.
A device that converts energy from one form to another, such as a microphone (sound to electrical) or loudspeaker (electrical to sound).
A device that uses the motor effect in a coil in a magnetic field to convert an alternating current into sound waves.
A circuit that increases the amplitude of an electrical signal without changing its frequency.
The force on a current-carrying conductor placed in a magnetic field, perpendicular to the conductor.

worked.ans: Sound waves make the diaphragm vibrate, which moves the attached coil to and fro in the magnetic field of a permanent magnet. The coil cuts field lines, so a potential difference is induced (generator effect). As the coil moves in and out the pd keeps reversing, giving an alternating current with the same frequency as the sound wave.
worked.q: Explain how a moving-coil microphone changes sound into an electrical signal. [4 marks]
steps: Sound waves are pressure variations that push and pull on the diaphragm, making it vibrate at the same frequency as the sound.
The coil is fixed to the diaphragm so it moves backwards and forwards in the field of the permanent magnet.
The moving coil cuts magnetic field lines: a potential difference is induced across the coil (generator effect).
The direction of movement reverses continually, so the induced pd and current are alternating with the same frequency as the sound.

worked.q: A microphone is connected to an oscilloscope. A steady note produces a trace with 5 complete waves across a time of 20 ms. (a) Calculate the frequency of the sound. (b) A second note gives a trace with 10 complete waves in 20 ms and the same height. Compare the second note with the first. (c) The speed of sound is 340 m/s. Calculate the wavelength of the first note. [5 marks]
steps: (a) Time for one wave: T = 20 ms ÷ 5 = 4 ms = 0.004 s.
(b) 10 waves in the same time: T = 2 ms = 0.002 s, so f = 500 Hz. Same height means same amplitude.

worked.ans: Both devices contain a coil in the magnetic field of a permanent magnet attached to a thin diaphragm or cone, but they are opposite. In a microphone, sound waves vibrate the diaphragm and coil, so the coil cuts the field lines and a potential difference is induced (generator effect); the changing direction of movement produces an alternating current of the same frequency as the sound. In a loudspeaker an alternating current flows through the coil in the field, so the motor effect exerts a force on the coil; because the current alternates, the force alternates, making the cone vibrate and produce sound of the same frequency as the current. The microphone transfers sound energy to electrical energy; the loudspeaker transfers electrical energy to sound energy.
worked.q: Compare how a moving-coil microphone and a loudspeaker work. [6 marks]
steps: Similar parts: both have a coil, a permanent magnet and a diaphragm/cone.
Microphone: sound makes diaphragm and coil move in the field → generator effect → pd induced → alternating current.
Loudspeaker: a.c. flows in coil in the field → motor effect → force on the coil that alternates in direction → cone vibrates → sound.
Energy transfer: sound → electrical in a microphone; electrical → sound in a loudspeaker.
Frequency link: current frequency = sound frequency in both.
